name: Emotional
def: Coping effectively with life and creating satisfying relationships.
lesson: Before mending, a kintsugi artist traces the entire crack, even the hairline parts. Feelings work the same way: you can’t repair what you won’t look at.
crack: Stress before a big test. Feeling overwhelmed, anxious or down.
staples: Bottling it up, venting online, pretending you’re fine.
gold: Name the feeling, journal it, talk to someone you trust.
extra: Try this: name the feeling in one word before you react.
note: Emotional wellness is noticing and handling feelings. Talking to a trusted adult or counselor is gold, not weakness.
photo: A 1500s Korean tea bowl. Every hairline crack is traced in gold.

name: Spiritual
def: Expanding a sense of purpose and meaning in life.
lesson: Wabi-sabi finds beauty in what is imperfect and changing. A meaningful life doesn’t come from being flawless; it comes from what you value.
crack: Feeling lost, or unsure about what really matters to you.
staples: Numbing out, or just going along with the crowd.
gold: Reflect on your values, practice gratitude, take quiet time.
extra: Try this: write down three things you’re grateful for tonight.
note: Spiritual wellness isn't only religion. It's purpose, values and meaning.
photo: A raku tea bowl: simple, uneven, and treasured for it.

name: Intellectual
def: Recognizing creative abilities and finding ways to expand knowledge and skills.
lesson: When a piece is lost, the artist builds a new one from lacquer and gold. Learning is how you build the pieces you don’t have yet.
crack: Falling behind, or feeling like you’re “not smart enough.”
staples: Copying homework, cramming the night before, giving up.
gold: Ask for help, break work into small steps, explore what interests you.
extra: Try this: add one word to “I can’t do this” → “I can’t do this yet.”
note: Struggling in a class is a crack, not a verdict.
photo: A lost section rebuilt in lacquer: building what is missing.

name: Physical
def: Recognizing the need for physical activity, healthy foods, and sleep.
lesson: Repair happens a little at a time
Kintsugi is done in thin layers, and each must cure before the next. Your body repairs the same way: through sleep, food and movement, every day.
crack: Always tired, run down, or getting sick.
gold: A steady sleep routine, movement you enjoy, regular meals and water.
extra: Did you know? Teens 13–18 need 8–10 hours of sleep a night and at least 60 minutes of activity a day.
note: Sources: American Academy of Sleep Medicine (sleep), CDC (activity). Energy drinks and all-nighters are classic staples.
photo: A teapot lid mended one careful layer at a time.

name: Environmental
def: Good health by occupying pleasant, stimulating environments that support well-being.
lesson: Urushi only hardens inside a warm, humid cabinet called a furo. Repair needs the right surroundings, and so do you.
crack: A chaotic space, constant noise, too much screen time.
staples: Escaping into your phone for hours.
gold: Create one calm space, get outside, unplug for a set time.
extra: Try this: ten minutes outside, or clear one surface in your room.
note: Environmental wellness includes digital spaces too.
photo: The urushi tree. Repair depends on what grows around it.

name: Financial
def: Satisfaction with current and future financial situations.
lesson: Kintsugi repairs instead of replacing. Before reaching for something new, notice the value of what you already have.
crack: Pressure to keep up with what everyone else has.
staples: Impulse buying, or borrowing money you can’t pay back.
gold: Know your needs vs. wants, and set a small savings goal.
extra: Try this: before you buy, wait 24 hours and ask “need or want?”
note: For teens, financial wellness is mostly about needs vs. wants and pressure.
photo: A cup about 900 years old. Someone chose to repair it instead of replacing it.

name: Occupational
def: Personal satisfaction and enrichment from one’s work.
lesson: Kintsugi takes long practice to master. Purpose grows from doing something you care about, and getting better at it one repair at a time.
crack: No idea what you want to do. Pressure about the future.
staples: Comparing yourself to everyone else’s highlight reel.
gold: Try a club, a part-time job or volunteering. Talk to a counselor.
extra: Try this: ask an adult you admire how they found their work.
note: For students, 'work' includes school, clubs, jobs and volunteering.
photo: A modern kintsugi cup by artist Chiara Lorenzetti.

name: Social
def: Developing a sense of connection, belonging, and a well-developed support system.
lesson: In a joint call, a gap is filled with a piece from a different bowl. The people around you can hold the pieces you’re missing.
crack: A falling-out with friends, or feeling left out.
gold: Have the honest conversation. Find your people. Join something.
extra: Did you know? In a 2021 CDC survey, students who felt connected at school were less likely to feel persistently sad or hopeless (35% vs. 53%).
note: Source: CDC Adolescent Behaviors and Experiences Survey, 2021.
photo: Tea is shared: a tea ceremony is never for one person.
